I call the meeting to order. Excellencies, heads of state and government, distinguished ministers, leaders of CVF partner institutions, colleagues, brothers and sisters, friends, good afternoon and welcome to the fourth CVF Leaders Meeting. I am Ambassador Liz Thompson from Barbados, the Sherpa of Prime Minister Mottley to the CVF V20, and it is my privilege on her behalf to welcome you here today as we gather in the margins of this 81st session of the UN General Assembly. This year, our meeting is convened under the theme of development, reset and cooperation. This is more than a call for a policy pivot. It is, in fact, a recognition that incremental adjustments are no longer sufficient to address the scale and interconnectedness of the poly crises which we face. Resilience, prosperity, equity, and partnership must no longer be treated as aspirational at the margins of development policy. They must become central to its achievement. Excellencies, for the countries we represent, the consequences of inaction are immoral, and they're also already being felt across our economies and communities. The moment before us calls for a different approach that anticipates risks, strengthens resilience, and delivers financing at the scale and at the speed which we need. El Nino has formed in the tropical Pacific and forecasters now assign probability that it will reach super El Nino intensity in October to December, reaching a peak. An event of this magnitude would rank among the most significant since records began in 1950. Already, I'm informed that August The monthly global average temperature reached 1.65 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, ranking it with 2023 as the hottest year in recorded history. But what does this mean for the 1.5 Paris limit? It means that we are facing a year of climate disasters and that it is no longer for us an issue of a remote contingency. It must become central to planning for the reality of the year ahead of us. It underscores the imperative of pre-arranged finance. Resources that are mobilized before crisis strikes rather than assembled after its consequences have already taken hold. And this is why today's meeting is focused on three pivotal issues. The first is the vulnerability to viability or V2V compact, our strategic partnership with 16 developing finance institutions so far led by the government of Barbados together with the OPEC Fund for International Development whose president was is in the room. The second is the Lifeline Fund, a multi-regional liquidity arrangement we are designing to meet the needs of members facing balance of payments pressures following tropical cyclones, floods, and droughts. The third is the CVF leaders declaration and member business, including an open call to Asia and the Pacific for the next CVF presidency and an update on the CVF second secretary general. Together, these remarks are the development reset in practice. moving from vulnerability to viability, from reactive crisis management to anticipatory action, and from fragmented support to coordinated cooperation. We will also welcome at this meeting three new members into our family, Zambia, the Central African Republic, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, whose Prime Minister is with us. It is now my distinct honor to invite His Excellency, Dr. Abdulhamid Al Khalifa, President of the OPEC Fund for International Development and our constant partner in advancing the V2V Compact to deliver his remarks. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Elizabeth, and thanks for the invitation to speak in this meeting. The Prime Minister, Motley, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, three months ago in Vienna, we were proud to launch the Vulnerability to Viability Compact alongside the V20 and Coalition of Financing Partners in the spirit of South-South solidarity and partnership. We are committed to building on this strong foundation and deepening our partnerships. The compact is built on an important principle. Development finance should be more accessible, more effective, and better aligned with the country's priorities. It focuses on three sectors that are fundamental to human development and long-term resilience, which are water, education, and health. Translating our shared ambitions into tangible progress would require sustained momentum around the compact four pillars. First, scaling concessionality. There is a scope to harmonize lending maturities and pricing criteria, taking into account country-specific debt sustainability constraints and the need for financial sustainability by financial institutions. Dialogue with donor countries on eligibility criteria would also be important. Second, Mobilizing private capital. Risk sharing instruments and credit enhancement can help improve the viability of investment and crowd in private capital. Third, strengthening country ownership. Financing is most effective when it supports country-led systems and is closely aligned with national strategies. and development plans. This is essential for strengthening implementation and lasting results. Fourth, advancing shock-responsive instruments. We see considerable scope for partners to expand the use of flexible financial instruments that help countries sustain essential public services during and after crisis. Allow me to briefly outline the OPIC Fund's engagement in the Compact's priorities. On health, we are expanding our partnerships with a number of organizations, including the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Rays of Hope initiative to establish cancer treatment centers. Following the first approval in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Preparations are advancing in Liberia and other countries. We are keen to extend this cooperation and welcome proposals from interested V20 countries. On education, together with our partners in the Arab Coordination Group, we will today unveil $1 billion dollar blended finance facility with the Global Partnership for Education. The facility is ready to work with V20 countries to translate national education priorities into investable programs. On water, we are expanding our engagement through the Water Forward Agenda and our Green Blue Connect Initiative. combining water security, climate resilience, and related development priorities. Through our Island Resilience Facility, we are working with regional organization in small island developing states to identify and develop adaptation projects. These initiatives provide practical platform for working with V20 countries to translate water and the climate priorities into investment-ready projects. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to support progress across all four pillars of the Compact, the OPEC Fund and Barbados will consult closely on the areas in which further technical work would be most useful and most effective. Our aim is to move toward practical recommendations that can improve access to finance and support implementation at the country level. I am convinced that working together, we can translate our determination to turn vulnerability into viability into meaningful and lasting progress. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Dr. Alifa. Thank you for not just your remarks, but for your leadership and your continued commitment to climate-vulnerable countries and helping to support us build sustainable economies. We will now have some updates from the CVF V20 Secretariat.

Thank you, Ambassador Thompson. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I will be brief. I have four points. Third, the science and health agenda, briefings on critical climate issues are circulating, including regular updates on El Nino. We are moving forward as well on coral reefs, high mountains, tropical forests, climate and health, and other focus areas put forward by the presidency and the membership. He served as the 48th President of Costa Rica from 2018 to 2022. In 2022, he received the National Geographic Society Planetary Leadership Award. He is Professor of Practice at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University in Boston. Thank you. Back to you, Ambassador.

Thank you. Ambassador Thompson, the Prime Minister of Barbados, Excellency Mayor Motley, Excellency Heads of State and Government, Dr. Abdulhamid Khalifa, fellow Troca members, colleagues, friends, good afternoon. I am honored to speak today on behalf of my president, His Excellency John Dramani Mahama, the president of the Republic of Ghana. On behalf of His Excellency John Dramani Mahama, Ghana fully support the declaration before us. I thank you very much.
I thank his Excellency Minister Esifoo and now invite the distinguished representative of the Prime Minister of Bangladesh, Dr. Simon Pervez, to make his remarks.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. I thank the CVF Secretariat and the Barbados Presidency for convening this timely meeting. We gather here not just to recount our vulnerabilities, but to rewrite the story of climate action with justice, ambition, and solidarity at its heart. Bangladesh has long been proud to serve as a voice for the vulnerable. From the Dhaka Declaration of 2011 to the Dhaka Glasgow Declaration of 2021, our leadership has helped place loss and damage at the center of global negotiations resulting in the creation of the loss and damage fund at COP28. This reminds us, when the vulnerable speak together, the world cannot look away. Yet, excellencies, the clock ticks louder. Rising seas, floods, salinity, and cyclones already disrupt daily lives of millions in Bangladesh. For us, climate change is not tomorrow's headline. it is today's struggle of existence. Distinguished delegates, I welcome the central focus on advancing the Vulnerability to Viability V2V Compact. We also express our strong support for the Lifeline Fund, designed to provide rapid liquidity support for climate-induced balance of payment stress. For countries like Bangladesh, where a single climate disaster can wipe out Years of development gains, such instruments are essential. We also advocate for a robust international financial architecture that supports all vulnerable nations at the recent Finance for Development Conference. We need stronger global efforts to keep global warming within 1.5 degrees Celsius. Bangladesh is committed to this effort. setting ambitious climate targets in our recent nationally determined contribution to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 20% by 2035. We are also committed to achieving 20% electricity generation from renewable sources by 2030. Today, our nations face a dual crisis of climate and finance. This unmanageable burden forces many nations to divert resources from health and education to service debt. From devastating floods to prolonged salinity intrusion, our people endured the harsh realities of a crisis they did not create. This cost as such the exigencies of daily life. Ladies and gentlemen, looking ahead of Looking ahead towards COP31, allow me to highlight some urgent priorities. First, set an ambitious new collective quantified goal on climate finance that is predictable, concessional and fair. Cheaper long-term finance must actually reach those building water systems, schools and clinics. Second, fully operationalize the loss and damage fund, ensuring swift and accessible disbursement, including mobility and adaptation support. Third, reform the global financial architecture to provide debt relief and concessional financing so that vulnerable nations do not have to choose between building schools or building cyclone shelters. Fourth, countries should not be penalized for progress. As our income rises, our borrowing costs jump sharply, while poverty remains widespread and climate risks keep growing. That transition should be gradual, not sudden. We welcome the declaration's call for exactly this. On leadership, Bangladesh fully supports Ghana's proposal that Barbados extends its presidency for a further year. V20 and the Lifeline Fund are mid-delivery, and continuity is critical to this group's effectiveness. Bangladesh supports the recognition of the CVF V20 as an observer to the UN and endorses the leaders' declaration. Together, we must ensure that climate action becomes a catalyst for sustainable and equitable development for all. The CVF was born from the conviction that the most vulnerable should not only be heard, but should lead. Let us leave New York not only with statements, but with commitments. I thank you.

I thank His Excellency from Bangladesh for his remarks and the Gaiden Troika for its continuous support. And I now invite Her Excellency Prime Minister Mia Mottley of Barbados, the Chair of the CVF 20, to deliver the keynote address.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. Excellencies, colleagues, friends. Let me thank all of you for being here. And let me thank our Troika colleagues, Ghana and Bangladesh in particular, for the excellent work that they're doing with us to be able to help us make progress. I want to warmly welcome the new members, Zambia, the Central African Republic, and indeed my dear brother from Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Each new member strengthens our capacity to defend our people's interests together. even as the climate crisis is denied and access to finance has been constrained. Barbados accepts also the call for us to extend for one year, recognizing that continuity is our duty now to ensure that we can move to the next level. I also want to, in his absence, welcome the former president of Costa Rica, my dear brother, as our next Secretary General, we have done much work in this same building to be able to advance the interests of climate vulnerable countries with respect to the climate crisis. Much mention has been made about the need for us to gain observer status to this UN General Assembly. Can I ask that we leave here with the singular purpose of canvassing we know what it is to Canvas because most of us are here because we learned the art of canvassing please Canvas now on behalf of CVF to ensure that we get that Observer status and let us also make one other commitment Go and bring one. Each of us bring one. Godwin, you have now come. There are still a few others in CARICOM who need to step forward. In Africa, my dear brother from Sierra Leone, there are still a few others who need to come forward. Dr. Pervez, in Bangladesh, you've stepped forward. There are still a few others in Asia. And if we can take this approach, then our aim is to have more members than half of the UN system. which means that we need to get to at least 96 members in order to be able to speak in this body and globally with the authority that we need to speak to gain the progress that we need to gain. And I say so conscious that we are really here with progress to report because others also have accepted the importance of what it is we're trying to do. I want to thank deeply, profoundly Dr. Khalifa and the OPEC Fund for International Development, who less than one year ago responded to the simple question, do we want to see change in the trajectory of development finance? And can we show the rest of the world as members of the global south that it is possible for us to innovate in the interests of our people? This came down to us accepting that we need longer-term concessional finance for education, health and water loans. Even before we complete the process, having signed the V2V compact in Vienna in June, and on our way now, as you heard from Sarah, to go to the annual meetings in Bangkok to meet on the 12th of October. Even as we are doing that, you heard Dr. Alkhalifa announce this morning opportunities in education, opportunities in water and climate resilience, opportunities in health, without us waiting to reach the final destination in order to be able to give assistance to our member states. This is exactly what we want to see. For those who have forgotten, the four pillars upon which the V2V compact stand, of course, is scaling up the concessionality in those three areas of education, water and health, schools, clinics and water augmentation. Secondly, mobilising private capital, of which there is tremendous amounts within our countries, but because of our failure to appropriately mobilise it and blend it with what we receive from outside, we are not getting the best advantage of it. Thirdly, Having country ownership, we have complained for too long how others stood in Washington and determined what our priorities should be. This is an example for us to make our own priorities, not only in what we do, but also how we do it, so long as we respect the fundamentals necessary to support development finance. And fourthly, using shock response innovative instruments such as debt pause clauses, pandemic clauses, debt swaps and other things to be able to augment the amount of money that is available to us. But my friends, you and I both know that a compact on paper is not a hospital or a school, or indeed the ability to lay pipes that can carry clean water to our people. We need to move beyond that. And therefore the white paper, which is being prepared as we speak, will present a toolbox of options for countries, for development finance institutions, and for other stakeholders to consider. I really do want to thank the members of the Arab Cooperation League, as well as the other development finance institutions who joined to help us constitute the 16 members so that we have a credible platform upon which to bring this change in process. But that toolbox to which I referred will only truly be authentic if you have a say in it. And therefore, we need to ensure that it reflects what your needs are, not only what we assume that they are. And I therefore ask you to continue your active engagement as we move to Bangkok. The Secretariat is willing to hear your perspective, and we're going to try to incorporate as much as possible in order to reach that destination. I ask you, therefore, not to treat this as just simply another event that you've come to attend at UNGA week, but one that has given you homework and one that will require you not just to canvas, but also to reflect on where you think the toolbox can be improved. It is against that backdrop I also want to thank the central bank governors who very often are laws unto their own selves, but who on this occasion have recognized that they still are part of global civilization and that they want to be able to make a difference as well with the rest of us who are trying to lift heavy weight. That proposal, called Lifeline, is intended to be able to ensure that, irrespective of what other access you have to liquidity platforms, that we create our own liquidity platform within the V20 so that we can help countries adapt to the immediate realities post-disaster and to give liquidity when liquidity is most needed. is against that backdrop therefore that we really want to urge not only members but to also canvas non-members so that we can rapidly move not to the 500 million floor that Sarah mentioned but at least a 1.6 billion and preferably 2 billion dollars because at the end of the day at the same time that we are speaking our membership is expanded and therefore the sums of money that we use to capitalize Lifeline must be appropriate to the needs of the increasing membership that we are getting here. With respect to the lifeline as well, in addition to that, I'm asking you to make sure that you go back home and make sure that those of you whose central bank governors are not yet on board, that you ask them to please come on board on this lifeline proposal. because it is intended not to subtract, not to divide, but to add and multiply to your options and to your possibilities in the immediate aftermath of a disaster. I will end on this point. I'm told that there is in Africa, for example, the reality of at least 300 million beyond the 300 million that the World Bank is committed to providing along with other development financial institutions access to electricity for. At the same time, we are also clear that in the last decade, 15 years, we've seen the prices of solar and renewable energy storage, electric end-use technologies, the prices have fallen in some instances as by as much as 30% in other instances by as much as 95%. At the same time, we are seeing a far more judicious approach to the whole issue of energy, ensuring that we look at ways of being able to extend credibly what fossil fuels can do in a world where we will not all have access to the commodities necessary to be able to build out renewable energy. So while we work to maximize our renewable energy potential, we work to be able to get the fossil fuel companies to reduce their methane emissions and to be able to scale up the research on decarbonizing technology so as to allow a fair opportunity for development to be available to all citizens and equally as important, a fair opportunity for economic development to countries who have been told simply abandon the past and do not find ways of using fossil fuels to help finance their way to net zero. We know that we are complex beings complex biological beings. We can walk, we can chew, and we can think all at the same time. And that is what we're trying to do by getting the right policy matrix such that we protect the planet and people without necessarily submitting ourselves to zealotry, winning one battle and then losing all of the others. It is against that backdrop that we recognize that renewable energy has one major advantage over all others, that the wind, the sea, the water, is the patrimony of ordinary people. And if we can maximize the use of those resources, then it helps us in the management of scarce foreign exchange and be able to ensure that the enfranchisement of our people by investing in those areas that are theirs to participate in will ensure that we help move more and more of our people into positions of wealth through enfranchisement, while at the same time ensuring that we minimize the use of foreign exchange. And as we are seeing now with the conflict with Iran to minimize the extent to which the geopolitical realities are constraining our ability to access energy. For those who are on the east of the Straits of Hormuz or to the south of the Straits of Hormuz, for you it is a question of whether you could access product. For us in the Caribbean and in the Americas, it was less a question of access and more a question of increased costs, largely because of the geopolitical realities of our world. But what has happened since then? In addition to the Straits of Hormuz, we now have the additional choke point that has been put in place by reason of the Houthis taking efforts to be able to control the Red Sea. And at the same time, of course, we have the announcements from the Panama government that they are reducing the number of vessels coming through the Panama Canal in any one month because of the drop in water levels that will affect, obviously, the functioning of the locks. This is a trifecta. that will literally compromise countries in terms of their access to energy. And I hope that as we move forward on the V2V compact, focusing on education, water and health, we recognize the critical importance not to lose sight of the continued efforts to guarantee energy security to our citizens, predominantly through renewable energy, but also by encouraging those fossil fuel producers to reduce methane emissions and to scale up on the decarbonizing technology for commercial application. My friends, I ask you, therefore, not just simply to attend today, but to recognize that the work which we have put on the table for each of you is a little homework that will make our institution stronger in a way that I stand here today watching an institution that has grown both in size grown in mandate and grown in progress in terms of what we have achieved. I have every confidence that this is an institution on the ascendancy and it is up to us who are here to make sure that this is not only the reality of the 77 countries who have joined it, but that the other countries of the world recognize its importance and are prepared to work with us in the interests of saving planet and people. Thank you very much.

changing our climate, yet our people face floods in Freetown, mudslides on our hillsides, coastal erosion, and lost harvest. Your Excellency, President Beelo, I thank you for your brevity. I saw you truncating your statement, and I'm grateful that you did so in the interest of time. I invite now the Prime Minister of the Republic of Rwanda, the Right Honourable Dr. Justin Sinigaya Mba, to take the floor.

Thank you, Your Excellency Mia Amon Motley, Prime Minister of Barbados and Chair of the CVF V20. Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, Honourable Ministers, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. On behalf of the Government of Rwanda, I would like to thank you for the opportunity to participate in this important event. As a member of the Climate Vulnerability Forum, Rwanda understands our shared responsibility to respond meaningfully to the climate crisis. Like many countries represented here today, Rwanda's experience of climate vulnerability is from abstract. Our national vulnerability assessments show the exposure deepening year on year in livelihoods, in agriculture, infrastructure, and across our economy. What is more worrisome is that recent projections put the cost starkly, indicating that climate-related impacts could shave 5% to 7% of our GDP. And that's not a distant risk or a single disaster to recover from. It is a standing tax on our development, levied whether or not we caused the damage. This is precisely why the Climate Vulnerability Forum exists And that's why Rwanda takes seriously what membership asks of us. We support the CVF V20 leadership declaration and the operationalization of the Lifeline Fund. We support the push for UN observer status for the CVF V20 because the country is carrying this burden should have a stronger voice in the rooms where decisions about it are made. And we support reform of the international financial architecture because adaptation at the scale our vulnerability demands will not be financed on today's terms. We need concessional finance and investment that matches the urgency we are describing. But we also convinced that adaptation alone cannot be where this ends. We can build all the resilience in the world and still lose ground if emissions keep rising at their current speed. That responsibility falls first on the highest emitters, but all of us have a role, and Rwanda intends to play our role. That brings me to one of the fastest, most concrete levers available to any of us, which is the full implementation of the Kigali Amendment to the Marrakesh Protocol. Fully implemented, this amendment avoids up to half a degree of warming by the end of the century, and paired with improvements in energy efficiency, that impact doubles to a full degree. few actions on the table today after that much climate benefit for that much achievable effort. This November, Rwanda is proud to host the 38th meeting of the parties to the Marrakesh Protocol, marking 10 years since the Kigali Amendment was adopted. And today, here in New York, we are launching the Friends of the Kigali Amendment, a coalition to drive universal ratification, accelerate implementation, mobilize the partnerships and resources needed, and ensure industry delivers efficient, climate-friendly cooling technologies at scale. I invite you to join this coalition, and I invite you to Kigali in November for MOP 38 to help finish what the amendment started. So together, we can take practical steps to reduce the vulnerabilities we all understand deeply and make our countries more secure. I thank you so much. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Honourable Prime Minister. I invite His Excellency Dr. Godwin Friday, Prime Minister of St. Vincent and the Grenadines to make his remarks. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you very much and thank you, colleagues, especially Chair Prime Minister Mia Mottley, and thank you so much for welcoming us to this forum. And Dr. Abdulhamid Al-Khalifa, thank you so much for the tremendous support that you've given to this particular initiative. We are delighted to be a part of this Climate Vulnerable Forum. It brings together not just persons or countries who will aim to benefit from it, but in our case, we bring direct testimony on the front lines into this common struggle for human survival and economic equity. Thank you for welcoming us to the forum. We are a country that has been inflicted or suffered from hurricane barrel recently that destroyed a section of our country where destruction was total. Help us to continue to work in these forums and in others to make funding available to deal with these problems that we confront. We meet at a time when cultural heritage, and in particular cultural property, is facing increasingly complex and interconnected threats. Armed conflicts, the deliberate destruction of cultural sites, looting, and the illicit trafficking of cultural property continue to affect monuments, archaeological sites, museums, and collections across the world. What is at stake goes far beyond individual objects or sites. Cultural property carries the memory, identity, and dignity of peoples and communities. Its destruction or illicit removal represents an irreversible loss, not only for the country concerned, but for humanity as a whole. Illicit trafficking also extends well beyond the cultural sphere. It can feed organized crime and in situations of conflict and instability, contribute to the financing of terrorist groups. As a country with an exceptional cultural heritage and with considerable experience in confronting the consequences of looting and illicit trafficking, Greece has a particular responsibility to contribute to strengthening the international framework in this field. The deliberate destruction of monuments, the looting of archaeological sites and museums, and the illicit trafficking of cultural property are not isolated malicious acts offending individual objects. They deprive communities of evidence of their history and of part of their collective memory and identity. They destroy archaeological context and the knowledge essential to historical interpretation and understanding. Illicit trafficking and trade in antiquities and other cultural property represent the most widespread form of threat to cultural heritage, both in times of peace and during armed conflict. The international community is increasingly recognizing that this is not simply a form of criminal activity. but a complex of highly networked enterprise of global organized crime with multiple consequences and ramifications capable of resisting coordinated international efforts. It sustains transnational criminal networks and particularly situation of armed conflict often contributes to the financing of armed and terrorist groups. Protecting cultural heritage is therefore directly connected, safeguarding international legality and security, defending the rule of law, and upholding the fundamental principles and values upon which international peace and cooperation are built. Over the past decades, the international community has developed an important body of legal instruments to confront threats to cultural property of national and universal significance. The more recently United Nations General Assembly Resolution 79/133, adopted without a vote in December 2024, reaffirmed the importance of the return and restitution of cultural property to the countries of origin and called for stronger international cooperation in this field. Yet, experience also teaches us that law cannot operate on its own. Effective protection requires broad and multi-level synergies and operational cooperation among cultural authorities, police, customs, and judicial services. It requires provenance research, reliable documentation, and the responsible engagement of museums, collectors, dealers, and auction houses. It requires the rapid exchange of information across borders and close cooperation with UNESCO, Interpol, Europol, Eurojust, and other international organizations. and it centrally requires us to harness new technologies, interoperable databases, digital monitoring tools, and artificial intelligence, responsibly and effectively in support of human expertise and institutional accountability. Greece has consistently placed the fight against illicit trafficking and the repatriation of unlawfully exported cultural property among the highest priorities of its cultural policy. This policy is systematic, dynamic, and multidimensional. Our national institutional framework is among the most comprehensive, robust, and stringent in the world, while Greece has also ratified and incorporated the international conventions and recommendations for the protection of cultural heritage. Our experience demonstrates that tangible results are achieved through meticulous research, systematic legal action, persistent diplomatic engagement, and above all, international partnership built on trust. Greece actively contributes to shaping international policy for the prevention and combating the illicit trafficking in cultural property through its participation in international fora, the transfer of expertise and good practices, and the development of bilateral and multilateral synergies aimed at preventing and addressing the problem. These synergies open new paths and generate knowledge, new tools and practices that are gradually being adopted by an increasing number of countries around the world. The adoption of the Red List, which raises awareness and provides police and customs officials, as well as the wider public, with information on specific categories of cultural properties most frequently targeted by illicit trafficking, is a characteristic example. Greece was indeed the first country in the European Union to have its own such list. The consecutive successes in securing the return of Greek antiquities from abroad in recent years through cooperation with authorities and cultural institutions in numerous countries, and particularly in the United States, confirm in practice that trust and cooperation are effective. It is equally important, however, that these principles should not be applied unilaterally, but in every direction. They have the potential to become the starting point of a renewed and elevated relationship. They can build trust between states and institutions. Open new avenues for cooperation through joint research, the exchange of knowledge and expertise, the exhibition and transform an unresolved legacy of the past into an opportunity for partnership and shared path towards the future. Greece and Italy have demonstrated precisely this through the permanent return of the fagot fragment belonging to the Parthenon from Palermo to Athens, as the Deputy Minister Papadopoulou has already mentioned. Disputes concerning the return or restitution of cultural property cannot be resolved solely by looking backwards at the circumstances and the terms under which the objects were removed. It is a question of restoring the integrity of a unique monument of the world cultural heritage. It is also a question of ethics, of science, and of politics. UNESCO's Intergovernmental Committee has provided the forum and institutional framework for constructive dialogue conducted in good faith between Greece and the United Kingdom with a view to seeking a fair and mutually agreed solution to this longstanding issue. The Fayoum fragment has already been demonstrated that such solutions are possible. Ladies and gentlemen, cultural heritage has the power to connect generations, communities, and nations. Our responsibility is to ensure that it is not transformed into the proceeds of crime, casualty of conflict, or a source of division, but remains a foundation of knowledge, dialogue, and mutual understanding. This is a responsibility that Greece and Italy wish to advance together. It is a belief and a possibility that the international community must continue to embrace collectively. Thank you.

Greetings from UNESCO. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to begin by warmly thanking the Permanent Missions of Greece and Italy for bringing us together today. As the illicit trafficking of cultural properties has become increasingly sophisticated and international, we must recognize that these challenges cannot be addressed by a country or institution alone. This is why international cooperation remains at the heart of UNESCO action. UNESCO works closely with Interpol, the World Customs Organization, UNODC, UNITWA and ICOM, as well as with specialized police units, museums and the art market. The UNESCO 1970 Convention remains the cornerstone of the international legal framework for combating the illicit trafficking of cultural properties. More than 55 years after its adoption, the Convention has now reached 150 state parties. Together, we strengthen national legislation and inventories. Together, we improve prevention. And together, we build the capacity of customs officers, police, and museums professionals. The convention is complemented by the ICP-RCP, which provides a framework for cases of return and restitution, offering states a space for dialogue and cooperation. For many years, discussions around return and restitution have focused on challenges such as differences between legal systems, limitation of period, and incomplete documentation. While those difficulties remain, we are also seeing a greater willingness to cooperate and explore different forms of cooperation. One example is UNESCO's dialogue on new forms of agreements and cooperation. As digital platforms transform the way cultural objects are traded, UNESCO has brought together digital platforms, member states, law enforcement authorities, and other partners to make technology part of our solution. Through the UNESCO Virtual Museum of Stolen Cultural Objects, we are also bringing stolen cultural objects back into public view, creating another space for international cooperation. Ladies and gentlemen, these are difficult questions, touching on law, history, and identity. But culture has the power to create space for dialogue where dialogue is otherwise difficult. This is why, as we look to the future through UNESCO 80, we will continue to bring states, institutions, and experts together.
